props.title: The Major and the Minor
props.initialSlug: Woman poses as 12-year-old to afford train ticket

sections.content: Billy Wilder's American directorial debut The Major and the Minor established his genius for mixing sophisticated comedy with social commentary. Ginger Rogers plays a woman who disguises herself as a 12-year-old to get a half-price train ticket, then finds herself entangled with an army major (Ray Milland) who takes her "young" presence at face value. The film's premise - an adult woman pretending to be a child while developing romantic feelings - walks a delicate line that would be impossible to pull off today. Yet Wilder's sharp direction and Rogers' brilliant performance keep it firmly in screwball territory rather than creepy territory, while slyly commenting on age, gender roles, and identity in wartime America.

sections.content: The film sits at a fascinating intersection of 1940s genres and themes. Like Mrs. Miniver (1942) and Since You Went Away (1944), it addresses wartime anxiety through a female protagonist's perspective. But while those films took a dramatic approach, Wilder uses screwball comedy conventions - established in films like Bringing Up Baby (1938) and The Palm Beach Story (1942) - to explore similar territory with a lighter touch. The military setting and identity deception also connect it to other wartime comedies like To Be or Not to Be (1942) and I Was a Male War Bride (1949).

Most remarkably, The Major and the Minor previews many of the themes that would define Wilder's later masterpieces: identity deception (Some Like It Hot [1959]), the intersection of romance and cynicism (The Apartment [1960]), and sharp social satire wrapped in comedy (Sabrina [1954]). The film's sophisticated handling of potentially controversial material through wit and style became a Wilder trademark. SUBHEAD: Gender and Identity in 1940s Hollywood Comedy

sections.content: The film's exploration of gender performance connects it to other 1940s comedies that played with identity and disguise. Like I Was a Male War Bride (1949) and Adam's Rib (1949), it uses comedy to explore gender roles while staying within Production Code boundaries. Rogers' performance is particularly noteworthy - she has to convince both the characters and the audience that she could pass for 12 while maintaining her adult presence for the romantic subplot to work.
